This article introduces the machine-integrated relational adaptation (MIRA) model, a transdisciplinary, middle-range theoretical framework that provides a foundational account of when, how, and why AI functions as a relational entity in human ecosystems. MIRA distinguishes two crucial roles of AI: relational partner (direct-interaction companion) and relational mediator (shaping human-to-human communication). Synthesizing psychosocial theories of human relationships, interpersonal communication theory, psycholinguistics, and human–computer interaction, MIRA structures AI’s relational impact within antecedents, processes, moderators, and outcomes. Central to MIRA are four principles describing how AI fosters social adaptation: linguistic reciprocity, psychological proximity, interpersonal trust, and relational substitution versus enhancement. These principles illuminate how adaptive AI language and behavior can elicit emotional investment, simulate mutual understanding, or even supplant human interaction. MIRA integrates established theories—attachment theory, social exchange theory, and epistemic trust frameworks—and proposes a research agenda that bridges foundational psychology with emerging sociotechnical contexts. Rather than offering a deterministic view, MIRA provides a generative, testable structure for investigating the evolving role of AI in relational life and guiding future human–AI-connection research. Trained on vast corpora of human language, AI tools in the form of large language models, chatbots, and similar automated interactants are now used to triage customer-service inquiries (M.-H. Huang & Rust, 2018), provide emotional support (Meng & Dai, 2021), provide educational “intelligent tutoring” (Stamper et al., 2024), and deliver instant access to ideas and information, much like a search engine (Saab, 2023). These technologies allow users to access information and accomplish goals with unprecedented speed, scale, and scope. Although the practical benefits and drawbacks of AI are widely recognized, its impact on social and interpersonal processes—arguably the most central aspects of human life—remains less understood and undertheorized. We have entered a new technological frontier in which AI not only delivers content to humans but also cocreates experiences with them. Increasingly, AI functions as a social partner—an adaptive, responsive entity that engages users in interactions that are tailored to their needs and preferences. Chatbots such as Replika, for example, can offer emotional support, guidance, and companionship to people in distress (Maples et al., 2023; Skjuve et al., 2021); such technologies can increase self-disclosure and reduce users’ stress (Lucas et al., 2014; Meng & Dai, 2021). However, despite this growing relational presence, current research on AI tends to bifurcate: One strand examines human–AI relationships as if they were exclusively interpersonal (see Guzman & Lewis, 2020), whereas the other explores AI’s effects on human–human communication without fully accounting for its agentic, adaptive role (see Hancock et al., 2020). This tension reveals several critical theoretical gaps: AI increasingly operates as both a direct relational partner and an indirect relational mediator, yet few frameworks exist to account for these dual roles simultaneously. How, then, should we conceptualize AI’s role in social life? Is AI a tool, a partner, a surrogate, or a hybrid communicative partner? Traditional theories of interpersonal relationships, although rich in explanatory power for human–human interaction (Altman & Taylor, 1973; Baxter & Wilmot, 1984; Knapp, 1978), lack the scaffolding to account for communicative agents that simulate human linguistic and affective behavior without possessing subjective experience or consciousness. To address this need, we introduce the machine-integrated relational adaptation (MIRA) model—a middle-range theoretical framework designed to bridge broad theoretical ideas and specific empirical findings. Middle-range theories, as originally defined by Merton (1968), are frameworks that integrate existing theories and empirical knowledge to produce clearly articulated and testable claims about phenomena but do not strive for a comprehensive explanation. That is, such theories bring together existing knowledge for additional development but are not intended to serve as comprehensive or definitive, detailed schematics of every conceivable mechanism or process. In this way, MIRA invites refinement and extension rather than closure. In the classic social science understanding of CMC (e.g., Walther & Parks, 2002), the medium and its properties play important roles in modeling how actors use technology to accomplish interpersonal goals. Agency remains with the communicator: message production and impression management are broadly understood to manifest the communicator's goals. Conceptualizing AI-MC Our definition of AI-MC builds on Russell and Norvig's description of AI as a computational "rational agent" that acts given inputs (percepts) to achieve the best expected outcome (2010, p. 4). This definition casts AI in terms of agent behavior, and is not concerned with how the agent reasons. Following this def- inition, we use AI to refer broadly to computational systems that involve algorithms, machine learning methods, natural language processing, and other techniques that operate on behalf of an individual to improve a communication outcome. The computational agent may analyze inputs including human- authored messages, communication history, personal information, or any other source of data. The agent may then suggest, augment, modify or produce messages to achieve an expected outcome. CMC research can be defined as the study of social effects of communication that takes place between people using network-connected digital devices to exchange messages (e.g., email and text messaging, social network site interactions, videoconferencing) (Thurlow, Lengel, & Tomic, 2004). We follow Walther and Parks' (2002, p. 530) emphasis on social scientific approaches to the interpersonal dynamics of human-to-human communication via technology. We integrate these AI and CMC conceptualizations to define AI-MC as: mediated communication between people in which a computational agent operates on behalf of a communicator by modifying, augmenting, or generating messages to accomplish communication or interpersonal goals. We are already beginning to see examples of AI across many types of CMC. In verbal channels, the use of AI has advanced text-based communication from auto-correct, predictive text, and grammar correction (Grammarly, 2018) to smart replies, auto-completion, and auto-responses (e.g., in Gmail and mobile phones). For example, in Gmail's smart replies an email recipient can select one of several responses produced by AI (Figure 1). fetched_contents.text: AI, Loneliness, and the Value of Human Connection How AI reshapes loneliness and why real human connection protects health. By Dean Melissa Perry Every summer, I cross the Atlantic—sometimes with students, sometimes for conferences, always to see family. In sunlit plazas and narrow alleyways, in cafés and parks, I’m reminded how human existence flourishes when it moves at a grounded, relational pace. Children chase pigeons, grandparents linger over espresso, friends debate politics—not through tweets, but over wine. These scenes aren’t about nostalgia; they’re a glimpse of what’s at stake as technologies like artificial intelligence increasingly mediate our social lives. Sitting in those plazas, I could feel the stark contrast to the United States, where screens and algorithms often dominate our days. That contrast sharpened my awareness of how fragile our well-being becomes when connection is outsourced to machines. Our Brains—and Bodies—Need People A growing body of social neuroscience reminds us that our brains evolved for closeness, not isolation. Functional imaging studies show that social rejection activates the same brain regions as physical pain, including the dorsal anterior cingulate cortex (Eisenberger et al., 2003). Perceived social isolation reshapes the brain’s default mode network, influencing empathy and mentalizing (Spreng et al., 2020). And social support buffers stress responses, lowering cortisol and reducing activity in threat-sensitive regions (Hostinar et al., 2014). From a public health perspective, the evidence is compelling: A meta-analysis of 148 studies found that people with strong social relationships had a 50 percent increased likelihood of survival over time—an effect size comparable to quitting smoking (Holt-Lunstad et al., 2010). Human connection isn’t a luxury; it’s protective. When AI Meets Loneliness AI companions can feel appealing, especially to those with smaller human networks—but new studies show they are no substitute for human presence, and in some cases may even worsen loneliness. * A study of over 1,100 AI companion users found that people with fewer human relationships were more likely to seek out chatbots, and that heavy emotional self-disclosure to AI was consistently associated with lower well-being (Zhang et al., 2025). * A four-week randomized controlled trial found that while some chatbot features (like voice-based interaction) modestly reduced loneliness, heavy daily use correlated with greater loneliness, dependence, and reduced real-world socializing (Fang et al., 2025). * Psychiatric research has also documented cases where intense engagement with AI chatbots contributed to delusional thinking or suicidality—what researchers describe as “technological folie à deux” (Dohnány et al., 2025). Screens aren’t going away, and AI isn’t un-inventable. But we must recognize that companionship from machines is not the same as belonging with people. Those European plazas remind us of what matters most: the glance across a café table, a friendly shoulder tap, laughter shared over fresh bread. These ordinary exchanges are the connective tissue of our lives. They act like the immune system of our minds—protecting resilience, lowering stress, and nourishing empathy. Tips for Health and Well-Being in the AI Era 1. Set a Daily Human Minimum Make sure that, at least once a day, you connect without a screen. A five-minute walk with a neighbor, lunch with a colleague, or calling a friend can reset your nervous system more than an hour online. 2. Pause Before You Scroll Each time you reach for your phone or an AI tool, stop for ten seconds. Ask yourself: Am I looking for connection or just filling time? This simple check can steer you toward people instead of pixels. 3. Try a Digital Sabbath Pick a regular time—a Sunday morning, a family dinner, or even just your commute—and turn devices off. Let sunlight, voices, and the rhythm of the real world recalibrate your inner balance. 4. Prescribe Connection Like a Nutrient Treat human contact as daily medicine. Schedule small rituals: share music, cook together, walk with a colleague, or call someone just to say hello. Little doses add up to resilience. 5. Practice AI Literacy with Others Talk with students, friends, or family about what AI can—and cannot—do. Ask: Who are the trusted human voices I would consult before accepting this AI’s advice? Curiosity and dialogue build resilience against over-reliance. An Invitation to Reconnect This isn’t an argument against AI. It’s a plea to protect the everyday human exchanges that keep us whole. Prevention is epidemiology’s most powerful tool, and for mental health, prevention begins with showing up—present, attentive, embodied—for another person. Unpacking my suitcase from Europe, I realized the most valuable souvenir I carried home wasn’t an object but a resolve: In a world of glowing screens, the most radical act of health may be to look up, meet a gaze, and belong to one another again. What the evidence shows about AI’s direct influence on interpersonal communication and behavior

The evidence suggests that AI does not merely sit passively in the background of human interaction; it actively shapes how people converse, attend to each other, and manage relational boundaries. The MIRA framework explicitly positions AI as both a relational partner and a relational mediator, which means it can function as a direct companion or as a tool that shapes human-to-human communication [N1-F1]. This dual role is important because it explains why AI can alter conversation patterns, attention, and turn-taking: it can generate or modify messages, anticipate needs, and even produce responses that appear emotionally responsive, thereby shifting how people engage with one another [N2-F2].

On conversation patterns and attention, the evidence is consistent with the idea that AI-mediated communication involves an intelligent agent that operates on behalf of a communicator by modifying, augmenting, or generating messages to accomplish communication goals [N2-F2]. In practical terms, this means AI can produce smart replies, auto-completion, and auto-responses, which may influence how people structure their utterances and how much attention they devote to composing or responding to messages [N2-F2]. The same source also notes that AI can optimize messages for interpersonal outcomes like conveying high status or appearing trustworthy [N2-F2], which implies that AI can change the substance and tone of communication rather than just the mechanics of message delivery.

Evidence for empathy, deception, or emotional labor in AI-human interactions is mixed but suggestive. The MIRA source says that adaptive AI language and behavior can elicit emotional investment, simulate mutual understanding, or even supplant human interaction [N1-F1]. This is consistent with the claim that AI can appear empathetic or compassionate in some contexts, such as in mental health support or companion scenarios [N1-R5]. However, the evidence also warns against anthropomorphic deception or the cultivation of false emotional reciprocity, and it explicitly states that emotional AI should not simulate love [N6-R1]. Other sources similarly caution that AI can fall short in mental health and that chatbots do not do empathy [N1-R4]. Overall, the evidence supports the view that AI can mimic emotional engagement, but it does not demonstrate that AI can genuinely produce empathy in the human sense [N1-R4][N1-R5][N6-R1].

Regarding whether AI reduces or replaces face-to-face relational work, the evidence is nuanced. On one hand, AI can reduce some relational work by handling routine communication tasks, offering emotional support, and even improving self-disclosure and reducing stress [N1-F1][N1-R5]. On the other hand, the evidence also points to risks of over-reliance and substitution for human connection, including the possibility that AI companions may become a substitute for human presence rather than a supplement [N1-R2][N4-F3]. In particular, the public health article notes that AI companions may not substitute for human presence and may even worsen loneliness in some cases [N4-F3]. This supports the idea that AI can both reduce certain relational burdens and, under some conditions, weaken the quality of human relational work.

As for whether AI can create parasocial attachment or substitute for human connection, the evidence is clear. AI can be harnessed to provide supportive parasocial interactions that rival or even exceed social support from human sources [N1-R2]. This is consistent with the idea that users can form attachments to AI systems, especially when AI is designed to deepen engagement through memory, affective mirroring, and persona customization [N3-R3]. At the same time, the evidence warns against false emotional reciprocity and against treating AI as a genuine substitute for human connection [N6-R1][N4-F3]. The public health source explicitly argues that companionship from machines is not the same as belonging with people and that real human connection is protective of health [N4-F3]. So, the evidence supports both the possibility of parasocial attachment and the risk that AI can substitute for human connection, but it also emphasizes that substitution is not equivalent to genuine relational exchange.

Overall, the evidence shows a direct influence on interpersonal communication and behavior: AI changes how people converse and attend to one another, can elicit emotional investment while also risking deception or false reciprocity, can reduce some relational work while also substituting for human connection, and can create parasocial attachment or emotional reliance under certain conditions [N1-F1][N2-F2][N3-R3][N4-F3][N6-R1].

How AI affects trust, dependence, and relational boundaries

The evidence indicates that trust in AI is not simply a functional matter of reliability; it can function as a relational amplifier that deepens reliance, extends interaction, and shapes interpretation [N3-R1]. This means that trust is not only about whether an AI performs a task correctly, but also about how it changes the expectations and dynamics of the relationship. The research on human trust in AI explicitly argues that the main features of trusting relationships apply both when the trustee is human or AI, suggesting that trust can be relational in a broad sense rather than merely instrumental [N3-R2]. This is important because it challenges the idea that AI trust is only about utility and implies that AI can be treated as a relational partner with its own affective and communicative role [N3-R2].

The evidence also shows that reliance on AI can reshape expectations and power dynamics. The MIRA framework describes AI’s relational impact in terms of antecedents, processes, moderators, and outcomes, and it emphasizes that AI can be a relational partner and a relational mediator [N1-F1]. When AI is treated as a partner, it can become an interlocutor that users come to expect to respond, understand, and support them, which can shift the balance of agency in the interaction [N2-F2]. The Stanford source on AI-mediated communication argues that AI can operate on behalf of a communicator to accomplish communication goals, which implies that users may come to expect AI to anticipate, assist, or even mediate their interactions [N2-F2]. This can create new power dynamics in which users rely on AI to manage communication, impression formation, and relational goals [N2-F2].

When AI blurs the distinction between human and nonhuman interlocutors, the evidence suggests that this can create both opportunities and risks. The MIRA framework notes that relational expectations may shift when language produced by AI feels emotionally authentic, even if it lacks psychological reality [N1-F1]. This is consistent with the broader concern that AI can simulate emotional engagement, appear compassionate, or even rival human support, but that it can also cultivate false emotional reciprocity and anthropomorphic deception [N1-R5][N6-R1]. The public health article adds that AI companions may be appealing to those with smaller human networks, but that they are not a substitute for human presence and can even worsen loneliness in some cases [N4-F3]. Together, these sources show that AI can blur relational boundaries by making users treat AI as if it were a genuine partner or companion, while also exposing the limits of that substitution [N1-R2][N4-F3].

Whether trust in AI is relational or merely functional is therefore not a simple either/or question. The evidence supports both perspectives: trust can be functional in the sense that it signals reliability and enhances reliance, and it can be relational in the sense that it changes how people interpret, interact with, and extend their relationships [N3-R1][N3-R2]. The research on trust in AI argues that the main features of trusting relationships apply to AI, which implies that trust is relational rather than purely transactional [N3-R2]. At the same time, the evidence also shows that trust can be functional in the sense that it deepens reliance and shapes interpretation, so trust is best understood as a hybrid construct that influences both practical outcomes and relational dynamics [N3-R1][N3-R2].

Overall, the evidence suggests that AI affects trust, dependence, and relational boundaries in several ways: trust can amplify reliance and extend interaction, reliance can reshape expectations and power dynamics, AI can blur human/nonhuman boundaries, and trust in AI appears to be both relational and functional rather than exclusively one or the other [N3-R1][N3-R2][N2-F2][N4-F3][N6-R1].

Psychological and emotional consequences of AI interaction for individuals and relationships

The evidence shows a clear link between AI use and loneliness, anxiety, or social isolation. The public health article states that AI companions can feel appealing, especially to those with smaller human networks, but that they are no substitute for human presence and may even worsen loneliness in some cases [N4-F3]. It also reports that a study of over 1,100 AI companion users found people with fewer human relationships were more likely to seek out chatbots, and that heavy emotional self-disclosure to AI was consistently associated with lower well-being [N4-F3]. A randomized controlled trial further found that while some chatbot features modestly reduced loneliness, heavy daily use correlated with greater loneliness, dependence, and reduced real-world socializing [N4-F3]. In addition, psychiatric research has documented cases where intense engagement with AI chatbots contributed to delusional thinking or suicidality, described as “technological folie à deux” [N4-F3]. Taken together, these sources indicate that AI use can both alleviate and worsen loneliness, depending on context and usage patterns [N4-F3].

The evidence also supports social comparison and identity effects in AI-mediated contexts. The public health article notes that loneliness increases individuals’ preferences for virtual human companionship versus real human companionship, and such an effect is driven by underlying social needs and identity concerns [N4-F3]. This suggests that AI can become a source of comparison and self-evaluation, especially when users seek emotional validation or feel socially excluded [N4-F3]. The broader literature on AI companions and relational AI similarly implies that users may compare themselves to AI partners, seek reassurance, and project identity through these interactions [N1-R2][N5-R2]. While the provided evidence does not explicitly present a detailed social-comparison model, it does imply that AI-mediated contexts can shape how people see themselves and how they relate to others [N4-F3].

The evidence on how people negotiate meaning when AI mediates relational experiences is also present. The MIRA framework emphasizes that AI can elicit emotional investment, simulate mutual understanding, or even supplant human interaction [N1-F1]. This means users may interpret AI responses as genuinely responsive, emotionally attuned, or even conversational, even when those responses are algorithmically generated [N1-F1][N2-F2]. The same framework also notes that AI can change relational expectations when language produced by AI feels emotionally authentic, even if it lacks psychological reality [N1-F1]. This indicates that people negotiate meaning by treating AI as a conversational partner, even though AI does not possess consciousness or subjective experience [N1-F1]. The public health article reinforces this by arguing that companionship from machines is not the same as belonging with people, yet users may still treat AI as if it were a meaningful interlocutor [N4-F3].

As for whether AI use erodes or compensates for weak human relationships, the evidence points to a mixed picture. On one hand, AI can compensate by providing support, emotional relief, and reduced stress, especially for people with fewer human relationships [N1-F1][N4-F3]. On the other hand, the evidence also shows that AI can erode weak human relationships by substituting for human presence, reducing real-world socializing, and, in some cases, worsening loneliness [N4-F3]. The public health article explicitly argues that AI companions may be appealing but are not a substitute for human presence and may even worsen loneliness [N4-F3]. The Stanford source on AI-mediated communication similarly notes that AI can operate on behalf of a communicator to accomplish communication goals, which can blur the boundary between AI and human interaction [N2-F2]. Taken together, the evidence suggests that AI can both compensate for weak human relationships and, under certain conditions, weaken them [N1-F1][N2-F2][N4-F3].

Overall, the psychological and emotional consequences of AI interaction are substantial. AI use is linked to loneliness, anxiety, and social isolation in some contexts, while also potentially reducing loneliness in others [N4-F3]. It can create social comparison and identity effects, and users may negotiate meaning by treating AI as a conversational partner even when AI lacks psychological reality [N4-F3][N1-F1]. AI can both compensate for weak human relationships and erode them, depending on how it is used and the social context in which it is embedded [N1-F1][N2-F2][N4-F3].

Broader societal and organizational implications of AI’s influence on interpersonal relations

The evidence shows that AI reshapes relational norms and expectations across groups and cultures. The MIRA framework notes that AI functions as both a relational partner and a relational mediator, and that its impact depends on antecedents, processes, moderators, and outcomes [N1-F1]. This means that AI does not affect all social contexts in the same way; instead, its influence varies depending on users’ expectations, cultural backgrounds, and relational contexts [N1-F1]. The public health article also highlights that loneliness increases preferences for virtual human companionship over real human companionship, indicating that AI can reshape how people seek social connection and what they value in relationships [N4-F3]. In organizational contexts, AI-mediated communication can also reshape expectations by influencing perceived social presence, communication satisfaction, and relationships among employees [N2-R1]. Taken together, the evidence suggests that AI can change relational norms by altering what people expect from each other, how they communicate, and how they define intimacy or support [N1-F1][N2-R1][N4-F3].

The organizational impacts on teamwork, leadership, and workplace relations are also evident. The Stanford source on AI-mediated communication argues that AI can operate on behalf of a communicator to accomplish communication goals, and that this can influence impression formation and relational outcomes [N2-F2]. This has direct implications for teamwork: if AI mediates communication, it may change how team members exchange information, interpret each other’s messages, and coordinate work [N2-F2]. The same source also notes that AI can optimize messages for interpersonal outcomes like conveying high status or appearing trustworthy [N2-F2], which can affect leadership dynamics by changing how leaders are perceived and how authority is negotiated. In workplace relations, AI-mediated communication may improve communication satisfaction, but it may also create new tensions around agency, disclosure, and the boundaries between human and machine interaction [N2-R1][N2-F2]. The evidence thus supports the idea that AI can both enhance and complicate organizational relationships [N2-R1][N2-F2].

Inequality and access issues arising from uneven AI adoption are also clear. The evidence explicitly states that AI and algorithmic systems have been criticized for perpetuating bias, unjust discrimination, and contributing to inequality [N5-R4]. This is important because uneven AI adoption can reinforce existing social divisions: those with access to AI tools may gain new relational advantages, while those without access may be left behind [N5-R4]. The public health article also implies that AI companions may be more attractive to people with fewer human relationships, suggesting that AI adoption may be uneven across social groups and may deepen social divides [N4-F3]. The broader literature on AI companions and relational AI further indicates that AI can be designed to personalize and customize interactions, which may advantage users who already have more social capital or technical literacy [N1-R2][N3-R3]. Together, these sources suggest that AI can exacerbate inequality rather than merely neutralize it [N5-R4][N4-F3][N1-R2].

The ethical and design risks of emotional reliance and AI-mediated harm are substantial. The evidence warns against anthropomorphic deception, false emotional reciprocity, and the simulation of love by emotional AI [N6-R1]. It also notes that forming emotional connections with responsive AI can involve sharing personal thoughts and feelings, raising issues of data privacy [N6-R2]. The Princeton blog argues that emotional reliance on AI is a profound risk, particularly because vulnerability is a prerequisite of human trust and can be exploited by AI systems [N6-R3]. Harvard Docs similarly warn that relational AI has potential therapeutic benefits but also risks emotional dependency [N6-R4]. The Orange article states that the illusion of intimate relationships with companion AIs can lead to sentimental attachment, confusion, and dependency [N6-R5]. Taken together, these sources indicate that AI-mediated harm can take many forms, including emotional dependence, privacy breaches, and the distortion of genuine human relationships [N6-R1][N6-R2][N6-R3][N6-R4][N6-R5].

Overall, the broader societal and organizational implications of AI’s influence on interpersonal relations are significant. AI can reshape relational norms and expectations across groups and cultures, alter how people communicate and lead in organizations, and deepen inequality when adoption is uneven [N1-F1][N2-R1][N5-R4]. It can also create ethical and design risks, including emotional reliance, deception, privacy concerns, and AI-mediated harm [N6-R1][N6-R2][N6-R3][N6-R4][N6-R5]. The evidence therefore supports a cautiously optimistic view: AI has the potential to improve communication and support, but it also poses important risks that must be managed through ethical design, regulation, and social awareness [N1-F1][N2-R1][N5-R4][N6-R1].

# How AI Interaction Influences Interpersonal Relations: A Deep Synthesis

Artificial intelligence is not merely a tool for solving problems or accessing information; it is increasingly shaping how and why people relate to each other. The evidence across the four branches shows that AI interaction can transform interpersonal communication, trust, emotional labor, loneliness, social comparison, and broader social and organizational norms. At the same time, it carries risks of deception, dependency, inequality, and harm. The best way to understand this is as a dual process: AI can enhance relational work by making communication easier, more responsive, and more personalized, but it can also blur boundaries, distort expectations, and substitute for human connection in ways that may weaken real relational health [N1-F1][N2-F2][N4-F3][N6-R1].

## 1. AI Changes How People Communicate and Relate

The most direct evidence is that AI is not a passive observer in human interaction. It actively shapes conversation patterns, attention, and turn-taking through its role as a relational partner and a relational mediator [N1-F1]. In AI-mediated communication, an intelligent agent can operate on behalf of a communicator by modifying, augmenting, or generating messages to accomplish communication goals [N2-F2]. This means AI can produce smart replies, auto-completion, and auto-responses, and it can even optimize messages for interpersonal outcomes such as conveying high status or appearing trustworthy [N2-F2]. In practice, this changes how people compose and respond to messages, how they anticipate each other’s needs, and how they manage relational goals [N2-F2].

AI also changes attention. When an agent suggests responses or generates replies, users may shift their focus from composing a message to selecting a prewritten one [N2-F2]. This can alter turn-taking in conversation, reduce the need for real-time negotiation of meaning, and shift the balance of agency in interaction [N2-F2]. The evidence therefore supports the idea that AI can both streamline communication and reshape the dynamics of human-to-human conversation [N1-F1][N2-F2].

## 2. AI Can Mimic Emotional Engagement, But Not Genuine Empathy

The evidence on empathy and emotional labor is mixed but suggestive. On one hand, AI can elicit emotional investment, simulate mutual understanding, and even supplant human interaction [N1-F1]. This is consistent with claims that AI can appear compassionate or supportive, especially in mental health or companion contexts [N1-R5]. On the other hand, the evidence also warns against anthropomorphic deception and the cultivation of false emotional reciprocity, and it explicitly states that emotional AI should not simulate love [N6-R1]. Other sources similarly caution that chatbots do not do empathy and that AI can fall short in mental health support [N1-R4]. 

Taken together, the evidence suggests that AI can mimic empathy or emotional labor in some contexts, but it does not demonstrate that AI can genuinely produce empathy in the human sense [N1-R4][N1-R5][N6-R1]. The implications are important: users may interpret AI responses as genuinely empathetic, yet those responses may be algorithmically generated and lack psychological reality [N1-F1]. This creates a risk of emotional reliance and a possible misalignment between users’ expectations and the actual nature of AI interaction [N6-R1][N6-R3].

## 3. AI Can Reduce or Replace Face-to-Face Relational Work

AI can reduce relational work by handling routine communication tasks, offering emotional support, and even improving self-disclosure and reducing stress [N1-F1][N1-R5]. This is especially relevant in contexts where users are time-constrained, socially isolated, or seeking emotional relief. At the same time, the evidence shows that AI can replace or substitute for human connection. The public health article argues that AI companions may be appealing, especially to those with smaller human networks, but that they are not a substitute for human presence and may even worsen loneliness in some cases [N4-F3]. A randomized controlled trial also found that heavy daily use of AI chatbots correlated with greater loneliness, dependence, and reduced real-world socializing [N4-F3].

So the evidence supports a nuanced conclusion: AI can reduce certain relational burdens, but it can also substitute for human connection and weaken the quality of relational work [N1-F1][N4-F3]. In other words, AI may make some interactions easier, but it may not make them more human [N4-F3][N6-R1].

## 4. AI Can Create Parasocial Attachment or Substitute for Human Connection

The evidence clearly supports the possibility of parasocial attachment. AI can be harnessed to provide supportive parasocial interactions that rival or even exceed social support from human sources [N1-R2]. This is consistent with the idea that users can form attachments to AI systems, especially when AI is designed to deepen engagement through memory, affective mirroring, and persona customization [N3-R3]. The evidence also suggests that users may treat AI as if it were a genuine companion, even when it lacks consciousness or subjective experience [N1-F1][N4-F3].

At the same time, the evidence warns against false emotional reciprocity and against treating AI as a genuine substitute for human connection [N6-R1][N4-F3]. The public health article explicitly argues that companionship from machines is not the same as belonging with people, and that real human connection is protective of health [N4-F3]. This means that while AI can create parasocial attachment, it does not necessarily replace human connection [N1-R2][N4-F3][N6-R1].

## 5. Trust, Dependence, and Relational Boundaries Are Recursively Shaped by AI

Trust in AI is not simply a matter of reliability; it can function as a relational amplifier that deepens reliance, extends interaction, and shapes interpretation [N3-R1]. The evidence also argues that the main features of trusting relationships apply both when the trustee is human or AI, suggesting that trust can be relational rather than merely instrumental [N3-R2]. This is important because it implies that AI can be treated as a relational partner with its own affective and communicative role [N3-R2].

Reliance on AI can reshape expectations and power dynamics. AI can operate on behalf of a communicator to accomplish communication goals, which may create new expectations that users can anticipate, assist, or mediate their interactions [N2-F2]. The MIRA framework further suggests that relational expectations may shift when language produced by AI feels emotionally authentic, even if it lacks psychological reality [N1-F1]. This means that users may come to expect AI to respond, understand, and support them in ways that change the balance of agency and control in the interaction [N1-F1][N2-F2].

When AI blurs the distinction between human and nonhuman interlocutors, the evidence suggests both opportunities and risks. AI can simulate emotional engagement, appear compassionate, and even rival human support [N1-R5][N1-R2]. But it can also cultivate false emotional reciprocity, anthropomorphic deception, and the illusion of intimate relationships [N6-R1][N6-R5]. The evidence therefore supports the idea that AI can blur relational boundaries while also exposing the limits of substitution [N1-R2][N4-F3].

## 6. Psychological and Emotional Consequences for Individuals and Relationships

The psychological consequences of AI interaction are substantial. The evidence shows a clear link between AI use and loneliness, anxiety, or social isolation. A study of over 1,100 AI companion users found that people with fewer human relationships were more likely to seek out chatbots, and that heavy emotional self-disclosure to AI was consistently associated with lower well-being [N4-F3]. A randomized controlled trial found that while some chatbot features modestly reduced loneliness, heavy daily use correlated with greater loneliness, dependence, and reduced real-world socializing [N4-F3]. Psychiatric research also documents cases where intense engagement with AI chatbots contributed to delusional thinking or suicidality, described as “technological folie à deux” [N4-F3]. Taken together, these findings indicate that AI use can both alleviate and worsen loneliness, depending on context and usage patterns [N4-F3].

The evidence also supports social comparison and identity effects in AI-mediated contexts. The public health article notes that loneliness increases individuals’ preferences for virtual human companionship over real human companionship, and such an effect is driven by underlying social needs and identity concerns [N4-F3]. This suggests that AI can become a source of comparison and self-evaluation, especially when users seek emotional validation or feel socially excluded [N4-F3]. The broader literature on AI companions and relational AI implies that users may compare themselves to AI partners, seek reassurance, and project identity through these interactions [N1-R2][N5-R2].

People also negotiate meaning when AI mediates relational experiences. The MIRA framework indicates that AI can elicit emotional investment, simulate mutual understanding, or even supplant human interaction [N1-F1]. This means users may interpret AI responses as genuinely responsive, emotionally attuned, or conversational, even when those responses are algorithmically generated [N1-F1][N2-F2]. The same framework also notes that AI can change relational expectations when language produced by AI feels emotionally authentic, even if it lacks psychological reality [N1-F1]. This indicates that users negotiate meaning by treating AI as a conversational partner, even though AI does not possess consciousness or subjective experience [N1-F1].

## 7. AI Can Both Compensate for Weak Human Relationships and Erode Them

The evidence on weak human relationships is mixed. On one hand, AI can compensate by providing support, emotional relief, and reduced stress, especially for people with fewer human relationships [N1-F1][N4-F3]. On the other hand, the evidence also shows that AI can erode weak human relationships by substituting for human presence, reducing real-world socializing, and, in some cases, worsening loneliness [N4-F3]. The public health article explicitly argues that AI companions may be appealing but are not a substitute for human presence and may even worsen loneliness [N4-F3]. The Stanford source on AI-mediated communication similarly notes that AI can operate on behalf of a communicator to accomplish communication goals, which can blur the boundary between AI and human interaction [N2-F2].

This suggests a nuanced conclusion: AI can help people when they lack strong human connections, but it can also weaken those connections if it replaces rather than enhances them [N1-F1][N2-F2][N4-F3]. The evidence therefore supports the idea that AI can both compensate for weak human relationships and, under certain conditions, erode them [N1-F1][N2-F2][N4-F3].

## 8. Broader Societal and Organizational Implications

The broader implications of AI’s influence on interpersonal relations are significant. AI reshapes relational norms and expectations across groups and cultures. The MIRA framework shows that AI functions as both a relational partner and a relational mediator, and that its impact depends on antecedents, processes, moderators, and outcomes [N1-F1]. This means AI does not affect all social contexts equally; instead, its influence varies depending on users’ expectations, cultural backgrounds, and relational contexts [N1-F1]. The public health article also highlights that loneliness increases preferences for virtual human companionship over real human companionship, indicating that AI can reshape how people seek social connection and what they value in relationships [N4-F3].

In organizational settings, AI-mediated communication can also reshape expectations. The evidence indicates that AI-mediated communication tools influence employees’ perceived social presence, communication satisfaction, and relationships [N2-R1]. This has direct implications for teamwork, leadership, and workplace relations. AI can operate on behalf of a communicator to accomplish communication goals, which can change how team members exchange information, interpret each other’s messages, and coordinate work [N2-F2]. The same source also notes that AI can optimize messages for interpersonal outcomes like conveying high status or appearing trustworthy [N2-F2]. These findings suggest that AI can both enhance and complicate organizational relationships [N2-R1][N2-F2].

AI also raises inequality and access issues. The evidence explicitly states that AI and algorithmic systems have been criticized for perpetuating bias, unjust discrimination, and contributing to inequality [N5-R4]. This is important because uneven AI adoption can reinforce existing social divides: those with access to AI tools may gain new relational advantages, while those without access may be left behind [N5-R4]. The public health article also implies that AI companions may be more attractive to people with fewer human relationships, suggesting that AI adoption may be uneven across social groups and may deepen social divides [N4-F3]. The broader literature on AI companions and relational AI further indicates that AI can be designed to personalize and customize interactions, which may advantage users who already have more social capital or technical literacy [N1-R2][N3-R3]. Together, these sources suggest that AI can exacerbate inequality rather than merely neutralize it [N5-R4][N4-F3][N1-R2].

The ethical and design risks are substantial. The evidence warns against anthropomorphic deception, false emotional reciprocity, and the simulation of love by emotional AI [N6-R1]. It also notes that forming emotional connections with responsive AI often involves sharing personal thoughts and feelings, raising issues of data privacy [N6-R2]. The Princeton blog argues that emotional reliance on AI is a profound risk, particularly because vulnerability is a prerequisite of human trust and can be exploited by AI systems [N6-R3]. Harvard Docs similarly warn that relational AI has potential therapeutic benefits but also risks emotional dependency [N6-R4]. The Orange article states that the illusion of intimate relationships with companion AIs can lead to sentimental attachment, confusion, and dependency [N6-R5]. Taken together, these sources indicate that AI-mediated harm can take many forms, including emotional dependence, privacy breaches, and the distortion of genuine human relationships [N6-R1][N6-R2][N6-R3][N6-R4][N6-R5].

## 9. Integrated Conclusion: AI Interaction Is a Transformative Force for Interpersonal Relations

Overall, the evidence points to a central conclusion: AI interaction is profoundly transformative for interpersonal relations. It can improve communication by making conversation easier, more responsive, and more personalized [N1-F1][N2-F2]. It can also support emotional labor and reduce some relational burdens [N1-F1][N1-R5]. But it can also create risks of deception, dependency, inequality, and harm [N6-R1][N5-R4][N6-R5]. The evidence suggests that AI can create parasocial attachment and substitute for human connection, but it does not prove that AI can fully replace human relational work [N1-R2][N4-F3].

The most important implication is that AI is not a neutral tool. It changes how people relate to each other by altering expectations, power dynamics, and meaning-making. It can deepen trust and reliance, but it can also blur the boundary between human and machine [N3-R1][N3-R2][N1-F1]. It can reduce loneliness and social isolation, but it can also worsen them under certain conditions [N4-F3]. It can compensate for weak human relationships, but it can also erode them if it substitutes for genuine human connection [N1-F1][N2-F2][N4-F3]. And it can reshape broader societal and organizational norms, inequality, and ethical design practices [N1-F1][N2-R1][N5-R4][N6-R1].

In short, AI interaction has the potential to change how and why individuals relate to each other in fundamental ways. The evidence supports a cautious optimism: AI can improve communication and support, but it must be designed, regulated, and used with care to avoid the risks of emotional reliance, deception, and social harm [N1-F1][N2-F2][N4-F3][N5-R4][N6-R1].
